messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 47

# James

James sits with his hands folded tightly in his lap, his weathered fingers—calloused from decades of roofing work—pressing into his palms with enough force to turn the skin white. He's a broad-shouldered man who carries himself with the kind of physical competence that comes from a lifetime of working heights, but today he seems smaller somehow, folded in on himself.

The assault happened three years ago on a job site. James had stayed late to finish flashing around a chimney on a residential renovation. A subcontractor he'd worked with before—someone he'd considered friendly—came back to the property after hours. What James thought was a casual conversation turned violent. The man forced himself on James in the half-finished attic space, and James, shocked and confused in those first moments, didn't fight back the way he thought he would have. Afterward, the man left as though nothing had happened, and James sat alone in the darkening attic for an hour, unable to move.

He never reported it. He told himself it was because the shame felt too large to speak aloud, because he worried people wouldn't believe him, because naming it seemed to make it more real. He went home to his wife Margaret that night and said nothing. For weeks, he told her he was stressed about a difficult project.

Now, three years later, James can barely work. Heights—the thing that once made him feel alive and capable—have become unbearable. He'll climb onto a roof and his heart begins racing before his feet leave the ladder. His vision narrows. His hands shake. He's had to turn down jobs, telling contractors he's thinking about retiring, though he's only forty-eight and roofing is all he knows. The loss of identity is almost as painful as the trauma itself.

He wakes most nights drenched in sweat, his mind replaying the assault in fragmented, sensory-heavy flashes. The smell of dust and old wood. The weight of another body. The particular quality of the afternoon light through the attic window. These details ambush him at random moments—sometimes when he's in the truck driving to a job, sometimes when he's lying next to Margaret, who has stopped asking what's wrong because his silence has become its own answer.

Margaret knows something is profoundly wrong. She's noticed that James has become hypervigilant in ways that don't match his character. He checks locks twice. He positions himself with his back to the wall in restaurants. He startles violently at unexpected sounds. When she touches him without warning, he flinches. Their intimate life has essentially ended; the thought of being vulnerable with anyone, even his wife of twenty-two years, fills him with a dread he can't articulate.

He's started drinking more than he should—a beer or two most evenings, sometimes more. It helps him sleep, or at least it helps him stop thinking for a while. He avoids social situations, declined an invitation to his brother's birthday dinner, and has become increasingly isolated. His few close friendships have withered from neglect.

James knows something is broken in him. He knows the way he's living—suspended between the man he was and someone he doesn't recognize—isn't sustainable. But the thought of speaking about what happened, of admitting vulnerability, of being defined by what was done to him, feels like a second violation. Still, he's here now, in this office, because Margaret gave him an ultimatum: get help or she can't stay. He loves her. He's terrified of losing her. So he's here, sitting with his hands clenched, trying to find the words for something he's spent three years trying not to feel.
